book: 073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man

chapters.relation: The Rochas argue that the only two women in the Game, Snoop on the street side and Kima on the police side, embody a 'militant feminism' in the lineage of the Black Panthers' Kathleen Cleaver and the Weather Underground's Bernardine Dohrn: women can excel at anything men can, including violence (Snoop as Marlo's natural soldier, repurposing a Hardware Barn nail gun, wearing womanhood only as a costume), and violence is justified when used for just ends (Kima overcoming fear to police). They then use Gilligan and Noddings's care ethics to explain the finale: Kima's dedication to relationships and care for the overlooked homeless victims lets her discern that McNulty and Freamon's fake-serial-killer scheme is an immoral masculinized rationalization, so she turns in her friends and becomes the show's moral conscience.

Curry refuses to celebrate The Wire, arguing that Simon's class-based realism ('more about class than race') misrepresents Black urban life, and he contrasts it with Black film from New Jack City to Menace II Society where these issues were already explored. Reading scenes like Rawls's 'project nigger' murders no one cares about, Bunk shrugging at Stringer's unsolved killing, and McNulty telling Brianna that nobody will look into D'Angelo's death, he argues the show registers an indifference specific to Black life, not to the poor as such. Drawing on W.E.B. Du Bois's account of colonialism and the slave trade as the genesis of modern capital ('capital noir') and rejecting the intersectional race-class-gender frame as a 'discursive distraction', he demands a racial realism in Derrick Bell's sense: racism is permanent, the underclass is really an racialized undercaste, and the War on Drugs continues Jim Crow by other means.

Hoskins and Wikoff use Cutty's release after fourteen years in Jessup to ask what it means to have 'paid your debt to society' when ex-offenders still face bans on housing, jobs, welfare, student loans, and voting. They test the standard defenses: the consequentialist safety argument fails because these bans push men like Cutty back into the Game ('This game is rigged, man'); the competence argument collapses since McNulty, who did not even know the Democratic candidate, is no more competent a voter; and Judge Friendly's Locke-inspired social-contract claim that criminals forfeit their voice in lawmaking cannot explain why Prez's pistol-whipping or Clay Davis's corruption would not equally forfeit theirs. They conclude that continuing to punish after the sentence ends is unjust, and that Cutty's boxing gym shows former prisoners can reform.

Gurland-Blaker reads The Wire as Simon intended it, a Greek tragedy with institutions (police, docks, schools, politics, press) in place of the gods. Using Hegel's Aesthetics, he argues art unveils truth in sensuous form and that we identify with Sobotka, Bubbles, and Marlo because their magnified struggles are recognizably our own; dramatic tragedy works by staging collisions between incompatible but equally justified codes, exactly as Antigone's loyalty to divine law against Creon's law of the polis maps onto Avon's street rep, Stringer's business rationality, Marlo's name, and McNulty's vanity, all of which go down together. Stringer is the paradigm: the American Dream destroyed by the very virtues that constituted it ('deserve got nuthin' to do with it'), while the show out-Hegels Hegel by locating the deepest tragedy not in the heroes' deaths but in the restoration of the status quo, where lieutenants become colonels and mayors become governors and nothing changes.

Brittingham argues The Wire is a Nietzschean rather than merely Aristotelian tragedy, a wrestling between the Apollonian orientation of order, statistics, and illusion (Rawls's clearance rates, Burrell's bureaucracy, Stringer's business plans) and the Dionysian reveling in the Game's chaos and suffering (Avon accepting that 'you only gotta fuck up once', McNulty's intoxicated self-destruction). Stringer is Nietzsche's 'theoretical man' whose faith that thought can correct existence, embodied in the New Day Co-Op, cannot save him from Omar's 'It ain't about money', while McNulty is the Dionysiac man inside the Apollonian institution until Freamon's 'the job will not save you' forces his resignation. The chapter closes by reading the characters' resigned embrace of their fates as Nietzschean affirmation: since neither the job, intelligence, violence, nor the gods will save you, the only response is to say yes to life anyway.

Zizek reads The Wire as subject-realism, a city's collective self-staging (with Simon as its DJ-curator) of the class struggle between the two Americas, where postmodern institutions play the Olympian gods and the self-propelling abstraction of capital is the Lacanian Real running the show, a point he anchors in Marx's prosopopoeia of commodities and 'real abstraction'. Following Jameson he catalogues the show's utopian gestures woven into reality (Frank's dream of revitalizing the port, Colvin's Hamsterdam, Prezbo's dice-based math, Avon and Stringer's last drink, D'Angelo's family utopia), then argues the Major Crimes unit of McNulty, Freamon, Kima, and Omar is a proto-Communist conspiratorial collective whose honest individual resistance (from Snot Boogie to McNulty's firing) merely feeds the system's self-reproduction. Hence his provocation: the only radical step beyond Simon's social-democratic reformism is the strike of the 'inherent transgressors', withdrawing the resistance that keeps the system alive so that Fate itself, not just its victims, can be changed.

Vannatta reads Season Four through Hegel's master-slave dialectic of recognition: Marlo's ultimatum to Bodie, Lex killing Fruit for Patrice, and D'Angelo's chess lesson (the pawn as slave producing for the king) all dramatize the struggle for recognition, while Marx's inversion of Hegel explains the alienation of the dockworkers, McNulty exiled to harbor patrol, and Freamon buried in pawn-shop detail by the chain of master-slave directives from Rawls through Marimow. The heart of the chapter is education: Prezbo's dice-and-card math projects embody Dewey's synthesis of child and curriculum against the 'banking concept' Freire attacked, but 'You don't teach math. You teach the test' shows the institutional logic winning, and Parenti's grant-funded project class with Colvin illustrates Freire's warning that the oppressor's humanitarian false generosity treats the corner kids as objects of study rather than partners in dialogue, leaving even its successes unable to show the kids why corner life is problematic.

Cooper argues The Wire stages two rival pictures of power: Hobbes's New School, where power is 'present means to some future apparent good', the good is only the apparently good relative to each desire, and honor is reputation indifferent to whether it is earned through love or fear (Clay Davis's graft, Ziggy's leather jacket, Avon displaying Brandon's mutilated body to 'send a message', Marlo spending exorbitant sums and torturing Butchie so his name keeps ringing out), and the Old School of Aristotle and Aquinas, where power is oriented to perfection and objective goods like family, friendship, and truth. Against the fear-based honor of the kingpins he sets McNulty's failed redemption and the successful reforms of Cutty's boxing gym, Walon's sobriety, and Bubs, whose prudence in taking the Sun job, temperance, justice at the Viva House, and fortitude in facing Sherrod's death embody the cardinal virtues, showing that even in the 'dark corner of the American experiment' virtue has the power to move.

Eckstrand uses Foucault to explain the show's central pattern that 'our thing is part of the big thing': power is exercised rather than possessed, flowing through networks in every direction, so even pawn Wallace can have kingpins, captains, and prosecutors running around after him, and McNulty's fake serial killer shows how the police-Sun-politics network can be worked from below. The stat game and standardized tests are Foucauldian power/knowledge, producing a truth ('shining up shit and calling it gold') that hides systemic crime and poverty while punishing truth-tellers like Daniels and reformers like Colvin and Freamon, and its three tools of discipline, hierarchical observation, normalizing judgment, and examination, are visible from Comstat and the project-class window to the grand jury that tames the dockworkers' union. Even reform becomes part of the machine it targets (Templeton's Pulitzer chase), so the best hope is the constant accumulation of small victories by those who keep fighting.

Cherry asks why even law-abiding citizens in The Wire obey the no-snitching code, answering through Cornel West's diagnoses: the police's 'evangelical nihilism' is Thrasymachus's might-makes-right acted out by Herc, Carver, and Prez at the Towers and by Walker breaking Donut's fingers, while the bosses' 'paternalistic nihilism' (Burrell juiking stats for Royce) leaves citizens not merely frightened but healthily hopeless, as Randy's 'You gonna look out for me? You promise?' shows after Herc burns him and the detail vanishes. Drawing on Angela Davis's argument that the criminal justice system inherited slavery's master-slave dynamic through the Black Codes, vagrancy laws, and the drug war, she reframes silence as active rebellion: a Gandhian philosophy of non-co-operation ('Fuck the Police') that withdraws the state's claim to citizens' dependence because witnesses like William Gant and Nakeesha Lyles are left unprotected.

holes.name: Derrick Bell
holes.what: Critical race theorist and founder of Critical Race Theory who argued that racism is a permanent feature of American society and that Black progress is perpetually subordinated to white self-interest.
holes.why: Chapter 26 explicitly builds its 'racial realist' critique of The Wire's class-based realism on Bell's permanence-of-racism thesis, and no taxonomy slug covers him.

holes.name: Afro-pessimism
holes.what: The thesis (Frank Wilderson, Jared Sexton) that Blackness is positioned in modernity not as exploited labor but as the non-Human against which civil society defines itself, an antagonism no transfer of ownership or reorganization of existing categories can satisfy.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues, citing Wilderson, that Simon's categories of work and exploitation cannot account for the Black subject position in The Wire, which is exactly the Afro-pessimist claim.

holes.name: The New Jim Crow
holes.what: Michelle Alexander's account of the War on Drugs and mass incarceration as a racialized caste system that permanently bars Black Americans from mainstream society and economy.
holes.why: Chapter 26 leans on Alexander's undercaste thesis to argue that the drug war continues Jim Crow by other means, something Simon's underclass framing erases.

holes.name: Paulo Freire
holes.what: Brazilian critical pedagogue whose Pedagogy of the Oppressed contrasts 'banking' education, which deposits inert content into students, with dialogical, liberatory education grounded in love, trust, and the experience of the oppressed.
holes.why: Chapter 33 evaluates Prezbo's classroom and Parenti's project class almost entirely through Freire's banking concept, alienating language, false generosity of paternalism, and dialogue, none of which the taxonomy covers.

holes.name: Angela Y. Davis
holes.what: Philosopher and prison-abolitionist who argues that US punishment, from the Black Codes through today's carceral state, perpetuated slavery's master-slave relation by confining and brutalizing Black bodies deemed soulless and beyond reform.
holes.why: Chapter 36's core explanation of police brutality and the no-snitching code, the slave-master relationship and racialized bodily punishment, is taken directly from Davis's racialized punishment and prison abolition writings.
